From September 1 a one-carat lab-grown stone sold in Russia is a 0.2 gram stone. That substitution is the whole rule.

Government Resolution No. 657, signed on May 30, prohibits the word diamond and all its derivatives in any consumer-facing description of man-made material sold in Russia. The tag must read synthetic, or the abbreviation Synth. It covers physical tags, showcase cards and online listings alike, so a retailer cannot write on a website what it may not print in a store.

The banned vocabulary runs past the noun. Precious, real, genuine, natural, mined, mineral and eco-friendly are struck, and so are the colour and clarity descriptors borrowed from natural grading. What remains is a product that may be sold and may be set in gold, but may not be marketed in the language that has carried it for a decade.

The weight rule is the sharpest instrument in the document. Every reference point a shopper uses to compare a grown stone against a mined one, and every claim built on carats per dollar, dies with the unit. Russia is a small market and it is not acting alone: CIBJO is expected to mandate the same single word on September 4. Russia's contribution is that it wrote the rules down and attached a date.

Gold lost the day and won the month.

Kitco's Friday close, timed at 5pm New York, put spot at $4,041.70 an ounce, down $60.90 or 1.48% and the weakest session of the week. Across July as a whole the metal still finished roughly 0.5% higher — its first monthly gain since February and the end of a four-month losing run. Markets are shut until Monday, so this is the number the trade opens August against.

Friday had a single cause. The dollar rebounded from a six-week low and traders unwound the rally that followed the Federal Reserve's decision to hold, a decision that had carried gold above $4,100 on Thursday. Softer inflation and an unchanged policy rate should have been supportive. They were outweighed by expectations that the next move tightens, and by a crowded position being closed before a weekend.

For the bench the month is the only number worth planning against. At $4,041.70 an ounce, fine metal costs about $130 a gram before refining, alloy, loss or making charge. A retailer still quoting from a January card is short roughly a fifth of its metal cost, and a customer funding a new piece with old chain is working the same arithmetic from the other side of the counter.

Five months of falling prices ended without a catalyst, which is the most informative thing about them. Nothing was announced in July that gold did not already know, and it rose anyway.

The largest Rolex showroom in the world will be run by Rolex's own retailer.

Bucherer, which the brand bought in 2023, has confirmed it will operate the Fifth Avenue flagship in Manhattan — a store WatchPro reports at 43,000 square feet across four floors. That is more than four times the size of the current record holder in Dubai. It occupies the base of a David Chipperfield tower, and opens around the turn of the year.

The commercial logic runs through certified pre-owned. Rolex CPO turned over about $186 million in the second quarter, up 67% year on year, against total secondhand Rolex sales across all sellers of just under $6 billion. A single very large door holding new and certified pre-owned inventory under one roof, with the brand controlling both price lists, is the most efficient instrument anyone has yet built for taking that secondary market back from the platforms.

The scale invites a question about demand. Swiss exports rose 11.2% in June but fell 0.7% in value across the first half. Committing 43,000 square feet in the most expensive retail corridor in America against that backdrop is a statement about the next decade rather than the next quarter, which is roughly how Rolex has always made these decisions.

The square footage is the story only if you think this is a shop. The store that controls both the waiting list and the certified pre-owned counter controls the price of every Rolex in the city.
